extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, art-critics, clergy, and educated readers interested in ecclesiastical architecture and sacred ornament
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and deciding the fitness, purpose, and execution of ornament and style in church architecture, especially with respect to Byzantine and Gothic practices and their pedagogical and devotional functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to viewing distance
rubrics_metrics.description: All good architecture depends upon the adaptation of its chiselling to the effect at a certain distance from the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details must be conceived for their visual effect at the distance from which they will be seen; deep modelling that looks fine close-up may be wrong for distant viewing. A faithful illustration is nearly impossible because architectural expression often relies on distance-driven confusion within order and mystery in trenchant lines. Example/anti-pattern: attempting to reproduce St. Mark's archivolts at plate-scale will fail to convey the intended visual effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color and materiality as essential to effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of certain architecture (e.g., St. Mark's) depends eminently on its color — 'the most subtle, variable, inexpressible color in the world,--the color of glass, of transparent alabaster, of polished marble, and lustrous gold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color blending, material luster, and tiny mosaic tesserae (sometimes a quarter-inch square) are integral to the design and must be considered part of the architectural composition; reproductions or monochrome illustrations often fail. Anti-pattern: treating sculpture alone without color consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament subordinate to architectural purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament (such as vine-leaves) should show 'a studious subjection to architectural purpose' rather than direct imitation of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forms may not directly imitate nature but should deliver similar pleasure while serving compositional and structural roles. Example: vine-leaves that are not naturalistic but please like true vine-leaves because they are subordinated to the architecture's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of close folding and broad simple spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: In shallow sculpture, close folds and rich patterning must be balanced by 'broad and simple spaces' to avoid insipidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sculpture is necessarily shallow (e.g., spandril carving of an inch or two), use compact, architectural folds opposed by simple spaces (like a scroll) to preserve beauty and legibility. Anti-pattern: uniformly shallow carving with no compositional contrast becomes dull.

rubrics_metrics.name: No architectural element is inherently sacred
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'no sacredness in round arches, nor in pointed; none in pinnacles, nor in buttresses; none in pillars, nor in traceries.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate forms on their historical and social context rather than assuming stylistic elements are intrinsically ecclesiastical. Churches historically developed from domestic architecture; appropriateness depends on familiarity and application rather than mystical symbolism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitness judged by continuity with daily architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever Christian church architecture has been good and lovely, 'it has been merely the perfect development of the common dwelling-house architecture of the period.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A noble style must be applicable to both dwellings and churches; if it cannot bear daily use, it will fail as church architecture. Anti-pattern: treating Gothic or Renaissance as exclusively religious or secular without regard to their role in everyday building tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rich church ornament as legitimate offering
rubrics_metrics.description: Churches may be richly adorned as 'the only places in which the desire of offering a portion of all precious things to God could be legitimately expressed.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ornament in churches can be justified as devotional offering, provided it serves worship and is not merely display. Consider whether the congregation is familiar with beauty; sudden sumptuousness encountered by eyes unused to beauty may distract rather than aid devotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity of beauty conditions its devotional use
rubrics_metrics.description: If people are 'familiarized with beautiful form and color' in daily life they will desire and accept it in churches; if not, sudden riches may disturb devotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the social visual diet: where streets and houses are ugly, lavish church ornament may produce distraction; conversely, a populace accustomed to beauty will expect it in worship. Practical implication: cultivate everyday craft to support sacred ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byzantine pictorial requirement and its liturgical implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Byzantine work 'requires expression and interesting decoration over vast plane surfaces,' i.e., pictorial representation becomes necessary because the style leaves large planes to be filled by ornament or image.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Byzantine decoration both for its pictorial nature and the effect that pictorial art has on religious feeling; consider whether painting/mosaic will assist or hinder worship in a given community. Anti-pattern: applying pictorial Byzantine surfaces where pictorial art is inappropriate for the congregation's temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious art should lie between idolatrous craft and distracting perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective religious art 'lies, and I believe must always lie, between the two extremes--of barbarous idol-fashioning on one side, and magnificent craftsmanship on the other.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid crude object-idols that encourage superstition and avoid art so technically sublime that admiration of technique replaces devotion. Preferred forms include missal-painting, glass-painting, mosaics, and frescoes/tempera—media that instruct without overly seducing the eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale, color, and distance advantage of mosaics
rubrics_metrics.description: Mosaics of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries 'covered the walls and roofs of the churches with inevitable lustre; they could not be ignored or escaped from; their size rendered them majestic, their distance mysterious, their color attractive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For public religious spaces where the congregation must be addressed at distance, choose media and techniques (mosaic/inlay) that are legible, majestic, and resistant to distracting evidence of technical virtuosity. Anti-pattern: small tempera details that do not read at scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of imagery as scriptural pedagogy (church as poor man's Bible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Walls of the church 'necessarily became the poor man's Bible'—the mosaics and pictures taught Scripture history to an illiterate populace more impressively than texts could.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select subjects and compositions that narrate biblical history clearly and coherently for catechesis; imagery should be pedagogically ordered and intelligible rather than merely decorative. Example: sequence in the atrium leading catechumen through Old Testament history to the Fall of the Manna as a typological lead-in to Christ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legibility and prominence of inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Old architects were 'sure of readers' and wrote expecting inscriptions to be read; inscriptions must be 'large and clear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including textual elements in architecture, ensure size and clarity appropriate to the expected viewer so inscriptions function as part of the building's teaching and meaning. Anti-pattern: tiny or obscure inscriptions that go unread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical arrangement of subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice and ordering of depicted subjects (e.g., in the atrium reserved for unbaptized persons) should serve catechetical ends, culminating intentionally (e.g., closing with the Fall of the Manna to point to the true Bread).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose narrative cycles so they instruct particular audiences (catechumens, the baptized, etc.), using placement (atrium, nave, dome) as part of the lesson. Practical note: subject-sequence matters as much as individual images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for untrained imaginative power
rubrics_metrics.description: There is great value in 'unpolished power' and imaginative gifts of folk craftsmen; the academy's polish should not be taken for the only source of artistic worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow and value work by competent local masons or carvers whose ideas may be rough but noble; do not discard expressive folk design solely because it lacks academic technique. Anti-pattern: excluding non-academically trained artisans whose work could enrich religious architecture.
